summary:
American Samoa is an unincorporated United States territory and stands under the full federal entry-and-documents regime. Federal executive orders reach the territory through federal agencies: EO 14168 on binary sex classification in documents, federal facilities and care funding; EO 14187 on gender-affirming care funding; and EO 14201 on athletic participation, the last paired with a State Department visa restriction carrying an SWS25 marker.

Since the January 2025 executive order, all United States identity documents reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department has stopped processing X-marker passports and markers that do not match sex assigned at birth; new and renewed passports are issued only as M or F on the basis of supporting documents; and passports already carrying an X marker remain valid until expiry. The X marker, available from 2022, has been eliminated for new applications. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked, and the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, with the policy contested in federal courts.

Marriage recognition is unsettled in practice. The Fono Senate voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after the House judiciary committee recommended killing it, so the territory declined a formal ban before Obergefell. In July 2015 the territory's attorney general said applicability of the federal marriage ruling was still under review, while Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands, Guam and the CNMI moved to apply it. In January 2016 the newly confirmed District Court judge Fiti Alexander Sunia told the Senate he had not read Obergefell, that the district court does not deal with the ruling, and that he would not perform same-sex weddings absent a change in local law. A 2026 law review article by two attorneys practising in American Samoa concludes that Obergefell does apply and that the territory would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied, while recording that no same-sex couple has applied to date and setting out a litigation route through the High Court of American Samoa, with the Territorial Registrar as defendant, and then the US Department of the Interior. As of July 2024 an on-island survey by Miami University professor Daniel Hall was still testing whether the local ban would survive a 14th Amendment challenge, indicating that the ban is treated locally as operative and its durability as an open question, more than a year after the Respect for Marriage Act obliged recognition of marriages performed elsewhere.

Trans people in the territory have obtained protection through national enforcement machinery. In September 2023 the US Justice Department secured a settlement with the American Samoa Government resolving an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee, and in June 2023 a federal civil action had cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity. In February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teen.

Social conditions differ from the legal picture. Fa'afafine, defined as people born male who embody both male and female traits, are described in university research material as a recognised and integral part of traditional Samoan culture, with colonial suppression followed by contemporary reclaiming of indigenous gender identities; the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (SOFIAS) was formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, re-anchored to cultural pride. Travel guidance describes homosexuality as widely accepted in Samoan culture, in contrast to Fiji, while noting that Samoan culture tends toward traditionalism and that reserved behaviour by people of all orientations is expected. Fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified at the 2003 committee hearing that Samoan fa'afafine do not seek same-sex marriage, citing Christian upbringing.
tangentialFactors:
American Samoa was the only US territory that had not moved to apply the 2015 federal marriage ruling, alongside which Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands, Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands had already done so; no marriage licence application had been made in American Samoa at that point either.

Contemporary travel commentary contrasts the territory with Fiji, describing homophobia as rampant there while presenting homosexuality as widely accepted in Samoan culture, and notes that the fa'amatai chiefly system structures social life across both Samoan nations. Local artist Dan Taulapapa McMullin has called the Samoan islands the homeland of fa'afafine culture. Accommodation in the territory skews toward business travel, with hotels such as Tradewinds in Pago Pago.

Guidance for trans and nonbinary travellers on document rules is published by Lambda Legal, covering which documents to consider, how name and gender changes interact with national records, and the current status of document updates; HRC's 2025 travel guidance sets out the passport posture for trans travellers under the same executive order. Both are secondary summaries of a policy challenged in federal courts, so their currency tracks the litigation.
localsOnly:
Employment protection has been pursued locally through national enforcement: the September 2023 Justice Department settlement with the American Samoa Government resolved an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee, and the June 2023 federal civil action alleged a hostile work environment against the territorial government on gender-identity grounds.

Marriage licensing runs through the Territorial Registrar, with the High Court of American Samoa as the first forum for any challenge and the US Department of the Interior as the subsequent defendant, per the litigation roadmap set out by attorneys practising in the territory. The Fono has jurisdiction over marriage law and rejected a prohibition bill in 2003; no same-sex couple has applied for a licence to date.

Community organisation is anchored in the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa, formed in 2010 from the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, operating explicitly as cultural pride rather than as a rights claim. Local testimony in legislative proceedings has framed fa'afafine identity as compatible with Christian upbringing and as not directed at same-sex marriage.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Obergefell v. Hodges is operative in American Samoa remains contested and unresolved: the territory's own officials have said they had not read the ruling or that it was under review, while a 2026 law review article by practitioners in the territory concludes it applies. No court in the territory has ruled on the question, and no same-sex couple has applied for a marriage licence, so the practical position is untested.

The constitutional durability of the local same-sex marriage ban was still being surveyed in July 2024 and no published result of that survey is available in this inventory. The scope of the SWS25 visa restriction attached to EO 14201 as applied to entry into American Samoa is not sourced here, nor is the current status of the ACLU's challenge to the passport policy in the courts.

Guidance from Lambda Legal and HRC is a secondary summary of a policy under litigation and may lag court developments. The February 2023 sexual-abuse charge involving a transgender teenager is reported as a charge only, with no outcome recorded in this inventory.
